folks have no interest to reduce the amount of repositories.

Me + obviously the guy from 
> (other than the naming concern that was raised this week after 6 months)?

+1 to Patricks comment.  Lets get this updated with the links to the discussion that have been had on this.  Mentioning "people" in the abstract doesn't add anything to the argument that this commit should be moved on.
Do we have data to back this up?  How often has this happened (other than the naming concern that was raised this week after 6 months)?

No data. People do not express themselves negatively about such things since its unproductive unless there is a patch. Same as creating github issues or bug reports.

Let's see what comments folks will make.

In general, this patch is more of an opinion piece. It's solving a subjective problem, not a technical one. It's still possible to develop OpenBMC with 100 or even 300 repositories. It's a valid architecture and there is no need to have any specific limit on the amount.

Just in this case, i don't feel like the extra repo is providing any benefit.
Why do we even have this issue?  We have well-formed dbus interfaces, right?  Are those dbus interfaces also changing?  That means you have to make a change in another repo already.

I'm not suggesting any specific change.

> That means you have to make a change in another repo already.

If you were to want to change how the led subsystem works in openbmc, by changing the dbus interface, that would be a change involving 3 repositories.

With this patch, it would only be 2 patches required.
"integration testing" isn't something we do at a repository level.  That belongs in openbmc-test-automation.

That was somewhat the argument for one big monorepo so this isn't new information.

But, we don't actually have trouble with people writing code.  We have trouble with people writing *good* code and we have trouble with insufficient high-quality reviewers to get the code merged.  I'm not convinced that merging code into bigger repos helps either of those statements.  

[There's actually an argument that it makes the code worse because it lowers the barrier to entry. :D ]

> There's actually an argument that it makes the code worse because it lowers the barrier to entry

Just switch to mailing list for development. Everything will be harder by default.



Let's not think about individual people or how to put barriers for them.
Let's instead think in terms of features and patches. Separate the patch from the contributor.


The barrier is not the problem, the problem is contributors being slowed down by having to communicate with 3 different maintainers who basically ignore each others existence and have wildly different ideas about how things should work.

The problem is the code duplication and wildly different coding styles that emerge when people are left to their own devices in their small little repository.


> we have trouble with insufficient high-quality reviewers to get the code merged.

Maybe this can be solved by having fewer (not monorepo, but fewer) repositories.
Which will increase the overlap between reviewers. When one goes to sleep, the other one wakes up and there is no freeze time when someone goes on vacation.

> "integration testing" isn't something we do at a repository level. 

Which is understandable given the considerable resource requirements to test a full bmc image.

However there is a lot that can be tested without building the full image.

For example using the PDI, the dbus interfaces provided by led-sysfs can already be created and then check if the led-manager can pick it up.

That then provides protection against people messing up the dbus path or anything of that sort.

Well, this isn't really ideal.  Part of the reason for separation is due to different levels of expertise.

'-sysfs' is the kernel-level interaction.
'-manager' is the algorithms around LED management for different LED policies.

> Part of the reason for separation is due to different levels of expertise.

That's easily done with partial code ownership over specific paths in the repo.

https://github.com/openbmc/entity-manager/blob/582d24f083af87c19d2e9d5c45561f7b535876cb/OWNERS#L44

If i remember correctly, the different expertise is one of the big motivations behind the invention of the path matching for the review and such. Github has something similar.

People can focus on their expertise without losing track of work done by others.

In the case of the 2 code owners for the repos being discussed here, i doubt the argument about lack of expertise applies here.
I generally think it's a good idea to merge those code bases eventually. I'm not familiar if something like was done before and what the best procedure is but this already looks like a solid start.

There has been discussions on the mailing list about monorepos previously:

https://lore.kernel.org/openbmc/?q=monorepo

I'm not really liking all the motion I see towards "monorepo by fiat" without solving the issues already raised on the ML.

Which specific issue is there in this case?

Many of the issues you described in that ML thread come down to the actual code owners following bad patters and merging the tightly coupled code.


I'm not suggesting OpenBMC to become a monorepo.

This patch is only about merging these 2 repos because i believe it will provide some benefit.


I'm not against having well defined dbus interfaces or separate processes, or being able to change one thing independently from another.

But enforcing that separation should be done consistently and not on an ad-hoc basis, right?
Should each program be it's own repo?
Each service?
Everything under 10000 LoC?
Every C++ namespace?
Everything that a user might want to opt-out of and not install into their image?

None of that makes sense to me. What makes sense to me is to separate it out if it is used as a dependency in multiple repositories.

I have not seen phosphor-led-sysfs used as a library or dependency to another program (besides led-manager).

A patchset that just copy/pastes the existing isn't the best place to have this discussion about the pros/cons of merging these.

I can imagine a case where I would be in support of this action, but definitely not without discussion with the maintainers of both repos, as well as discussion on how it would be executed.

As written, this patchset can't merge.  I fully support you starting a discussion with the maintainers and TOF around if this is the right direction, then if you don't get to the agreement you want, starting a design doc that can be voted on in the TOF.

Alexander, this is essentially the same design path you took with:
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/bmcweb/+/73627

Where you opened a patchset doing a relatively large "merge" refactoring without discussion or documentation as to why it improved things.  The review was ultimately closed with me (the maintainer) not understanding why it was needed or what it enabled for you, regardless of the code.

Opening these kinds of gerrit reviews requires a lot of folks to take time to review and takes time away from other things.  To prioritize both of our time, I would highly recommend starting by focusing on the "why" in your commit messages and emails, keeping it specific to technical details about why we would want to merge these repositories ahead of the mechanical, how we do this.


FWIW, I've pushed on a very similar track a long time ago, making technical arguments about why code should be combined at a much higher level.  https://lore.kernel.org/openbmc/CAH2-KxAJS_U8=meCxp8ue7n0bmnzeRpyZOPZpy0h1cFEbbz-HA@mail.gmail.com/

Feel free to use any content there to help you make your argument.
